Most nearly mean, underlined phrase or phrase options

items.passage: Documented by linguist Joanne Yager and colleagues, Jedek, a language spoken by 280 hunter-gatherers in northern Peninsular Malaysia, has a vocabulary ______ its speakers’ way of life: their community has no courts and discourages competition among children, and Jedek lacks indigenous verbs denoting ownership, such as “borrow” and “steal,” yet possesses an extensive vocabulary for exchanging and sharing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Consonant with” means in agreement with. The text says that Jedek’s speakers live in a community without courts that encourages children not to compete, and that their language lacks indigenous verbs for ownership, such as “borrow” and “steal,” but has a large vocabulary for exchanging and sharing. The vocabulary, in other words, fits the speakers’ way of life.

A.why_wrong: “Coeval with” means existing at the same time as. The text says nothing about when Jedek’s vocabulary or its speakers’ way of life arose; it describes how well the two match.

B.why_wrong: “Inured to” means hardened or accustomed to something unpleasant, which describes a person, not a vocabulary. The text presents the speakers’ way of life as something the vocabulary reflects, not as a hardship it has grown used to.

D.why_wrong: “Irreconcilable with” means impossible to bring into agreement with. A language without native verbs for ownership but with a large vocabulary for sharing matches a community that discourages competition; it does not clash with it.

sources.what: Lund University press release (2018): Jedek, documented by Joanne Yager and Niclas Burenhult, spoken by about 280 settled hunter-gatherers in northern Peninsular Malaysia; no laws or courts, children encouraged not to compete; no indigenous verbs for ownership such as borrow, steal, buy or sell, but a rich vocabulary for exchanging and sharing

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (the colon gives two facts about the community and two about the lexicon; the student must see that they agree, and must read “consonant” in its general sense, not as the speech-sound term a linguistics passage invites). Band-7 moves: all four options past rank 10,000; key a familiar word in a secondary sense; near miss inured to (wrong agent). Raw freq.txt ranks: coeval with 48,103; inured to 21,924; consonant with 36,494; irreconcilable with 30,930 (mean log about 4.5). Band-7 gate: 4 of 4 options past rank 10,000 and key past 20,000 (pass); the rarest distractor, coeval with, sits just under the 50,000 mark. Credited to Yager, first author of the 2017 Linguistic Typology description, and colleagues (the release names Yager and Niclas Burenhult; Burenhult already appears in another item, so only the lead author is named). Simplified: the release names more traits of the community (no professions, little violence); two are used.

band7.why: Option-set rarity at the band-7 level: all four options past rank 20,000 corrected (coeval with 48,103; inured to 21,924; consonant with 20,866 corrected, 36,494 raw; irreconcilable with 30,930; mean log 4.46), one band, key not the rarest. Checks 1 and 3 pass; check 2 just misses (rarest distractor coeval with 48,103, under 50,000). Two steps (two community facts and two lexical facts after the colon must be read as agreeing) and the key is a secondary sense of a word a linguistics passage reads as a speech-sound term. No distractor fits loosely: coeval concerns timing the text never gives, inured needs a person and a hardship, irreconcilable reverses the match.

items.passage: Habitual reliance on satellite navigation may cause people’s own navigational abilities to ______. When Louisa Dahmani and Véronique Bohbot reassessed a cohort of drivers three years after initially testing them, those who had relied more heavily on GPS in the interim exhibited a steeper decline in the spatial memory required for unassisted navigation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Atrophy” here means to weaken from lack of use. The text says that drivers who used GPS more over three years showed a steeper decline in the spatial memory they would need to navigate on their own, so relying on GPS may make those abilities waste away.

B.why_wrong: “Ossify” means to become rigid and unable to change. The text describes navigational memory getting weaker, not becoming fixed or inflexible.

C.why_wrong: “Proliferate” means to multiply or increase rapidly. The drivers who relied more on GPS showed a steeper decline in spatial memory, the opposite of growth.

D.why_wrong: “Coalesce” means to come together into one mass or whole. Nothing in the text suggests that navigational abilities merge; it reports that they decline.

sources.what: Dahmani and Bohbot, Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation (Scientific Reports, 2020): 13 drivers retested three years after initial testing; greater GPS use since initial testing was associated with a steeper decline in hippocampal-dependent spatial memory

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology, cognitive neuroscience). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (a steeper decline among heavier users, read as a consequence of reliance; key a familiar word in a transferred sense, from muscles to skills). Band-7 moves: all four options past rank 10,000 (atrophy 42,603; ossify unseen; proliferate unseen; coalesce 70,369; gate passes on all three checks), near miss ossify (rigid, not weaker). Hedged with “may”: the longitudinal sample was small and the design correlational, as the paper says.

band7.why: Carried by vocabulary, which the spec allows at one step: all four options past 40,000 (atrophy 42,603; coalesce 70,369; ossify and proliferate unseen; mean log 5.37), one band, key not the rarest; checks 1 to 3 pass. Logic is one step (steeper decline restates the key) with the key in a transferred sense (muscle to skill), like repudiates and ubiquity at band 7. Near miss ossify fails on one feature (rigid, not weaker); proliferate reverses, coalesce is unsupported; none fits a decline even loosely.

items.passage: Distant from highways, industry, and other human sources of vibration, Antarctica’s Ross Ice Shelf might be expected to be ______. Yet when Julien Chaput and colleagues analyzed recordings from seismometers buried in the shelf’s snowpack, they detected a virtually continuous hum: winds sweeping across dunes on the snowy surface cause the snow and ice to vibrate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Quiescent” means quiet and still. The text describes the expectation for an ice shelf far from any human source of vibration, and “Yet” introduces a finding that contradicts it: the shelf hums almost constantly. The expectation, then, was that the shelf would be quiet.

A.recipe: reversal: trait of the wrong side (ANT)
A.why_wrong: “Resonant” means vibrating or echoing with sound. That describes what the researchers actually found, a nearly constant hum, not the expectation that “Yet” sets against the finding.

B.why_wrong: “Buoyant” means able to float. An ice shelf does float, but that expectation would not be contradicted by the discovery of a hum, so it cannot be what “Yet” contrasts with.

C.why_wrong: “Friable” means easily crumbled. Nothing in the text concerns whether the ice crumbles; the contrast is between an expected silence and a constant hum.

sources.what: UPI (2018) on Chaput et al., Geophysical Research Letters: seismometers buried beneath the snow of the Ross Ice Shelf, data 2014 to 2017; as wind blows across the shelf’s snow dunes the snow and ice hum; the dunes are constantly vibrating; Julien Chaput quoted as lead researcher

items.notes: Subject: natural science (earth science, glaciology). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (the blank sits on an expectation built from the absence of human sources of vibration; “Yet” and the hum show what it was). Band-7 moves: blank on the expectation, not the finding; the finding’s own trait (resonant) is the trap; all four options past rank 10,000 (resonant 16,377; buoyant 10,544; friable 71,307; quiescent 26,072; gate passes on all three checks). The expectation is framed as a reasonable guess, not attributed to anyone. Simplified: the hum is about 5 hertz, below human hearing; the paper also tracks how it shifts with weather.

band7.why: Band-7 B3 shape: the blank sits on the expectation built from the absence of human vibration, and “Yet” plus the hum must be undone to reach it; the finding’s own trait (resonant) is the trap. All four options past 10,000 (buoyant 10,544, barely; resonant 16,377; quiescent 26,072; friable 71,307; mean log 4.38), rarest distractor past 50,000, so checks 1 to 3 pass. Buoyant is true of an ice shelf but nothing in the text, and no hum, contradicts it, so it does not fit the contrast.

items.passage: Sensitivity to sunk costs is by no means ______ to humans. In parallel foraging experiments devised by Brian Sweis and colleagues, mice and rats awaiting food and people awaiting short videos all became increasingly reluctant to abandon the wait the longer they had already waited, although that time was irrecoverable.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Peculiar to” here means belonging only to. The text describes tasks in which mice, rats, and people all became less willing to give up the longer they had already waited, which is sensitivity to sunk costs. Since rodents show it too, it is by no means found only in humans.

A.why_wrong: Saying that sensitivity to sunk costs is “by no means relevant to humans” would contradict the text, which reports that people in the study showed it just as the rodents did.

C.why_wrong: Calling the behavior “by no means harmful to humans” is not supported: the text says the participants kept waiting even though the time they had spent could not be recovered, which suggests a cost rather than ruling one out.

D.why_wrong: “Indispensable” means absolutely necessary. The text says nothing about whether humans need this sensitivity; it compares which species show it.

sources.what: Scientific American on Sweis et al., Sensitivity to sunk costs in mice, rats, and humans (Science, 2018): University of Minnesota team; Restaurant Row task in which rodents decide whether to wait for flavored food, a parallel task in which people decide whether to wait for videos; rats, mice and humans all exhibit sunk cost behavior

Sweis et al., Sensitivity to “sunk costs” in mice, rats, and humans (Science, 2018), PubMed abstract: in two parallel foraging tasks the authors designed, mice, rats and humans show similar sensitivities to sunk costs, resisting ending an activity because of the time already invested

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology, decision-making). Key letter B. Band 6 by design (plan cell). Steps: 2 (the negated frame plus the cross-species result). Distractors: one negation flip (relevant), one reversal of the passage’s implied cost (harmful), one unsupported (indispensable). The key is a familiar word in its secondary sense (peculiar to = exclusive to); read in its everyday sense (“strange to humans”) it still points to the key, so there is no second reading that favors another option. Raw freq.txt ranks: relevant 17,434; peculiar 1,920; harmful 22,343; indispensable 10,496. Simplified: the paper’s finding that the effect appears only after an initial commitment is left out.

fixes: added the Science 2018 paper (PubMed abstract) as source: it states the parallel foraging tasks and the time-invested effect, which the Scientific American piece gives only loosely
passage “awaiting flavored food” changed to “awaiting food” (the sources give flavors for the rat task only)

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target as the band-6 B5 pattern: the negation is stated outright (by no means), the key is a plain word in its secondary sense (peculiar to = exclusive to) and one distractor is a negation flip (relevant). Two steps (negated frame plus the cross-species result). Deviation from one frequency band: the key peculiar (1,920) sits under the distractors (relevant 1,600 corrected but 17,434 raw; harmful 7,289 corrected, 22,343 raw; indispensable 10,496); a common key under rarer distractors is the band-6 pattern, not the band-5 guard (which is the reverse), so left as is. No distractor fits: harmful and indispensable have no bearing on the rodent evidence.

items.passage:
The following text is from Edward Eggleston’s 1891 novel The Faith Doctor.

How to bear her dignity as the wife of a man who used the million as a unit [Mrs. Van Horne] did not know, for though she <u>affected</u> a reserved stateliness of manner, it did not set well on such a round-faced, impressionable little woman quite incapable of charting a course for herself. No show of leadership had been hers, but she had taken her cue from this and that stronger nature, until by chance she came in hailing distance of Mrs. Hilbrough.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “affected” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Mrs. Van Horne displays a reserved, stately manner, but the text says it “did not set well” on a woman so impressionable and so unable to chart her own course, who had always “taken her cue” from stronger people. The manner was put on rather than natural, so “affected” most nearly means simulated.

A.why_wrong: To affect can mean to influence or sway, but Mrs. Van Horne is not influencing a manner; she is putting one on that does not suit her.

B.why_wrong: To be affected can mean to be emotionally disturbed or perturbed, but here Mrs. Van Horne is the one doing the affecting, and the object is a manner she adopts, not something that upsets her.

D.why_wrong: A disease can be said to affect, or afflict, a person, but nothing in the text concerns illness; it describes a manner Mrs. Van Horne adopts.

sources.what: Text of The Faith Doctor: A Story of New York (Edward Eggleston, 1891; copyright 1891, D. Appleton and Company)

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter C. Excerpt copied exactly from one paragraph, trimmed at sentence boundaries (the earlier sentences about the Van Hornes’ railway fortune and the later ones about Mrs. Hilbrough are dropped); “[Mrs. Van Horne]” replaces “she”. Steps: 2 (the manner “did not set well” on her, and she took her cue from others, so it was put on). Band-7 moves: a common target in a secondary sense (affect = feign or put on, not influence); all three distractors are real senses of “affect” (influence, emotional effect, disease), so a student who knows only the everyday sense is drawn to Swayed. No distractor is a sense that fits loosely: the senses “to fancy” and “to imitate” were left out because she prefers or copies the manner in some readings. Raw freq.txt ranks: Swayed 5,327; Perturbed 11,243; Simulated 18,144; Afflicted 9,594 (mid-frequency set like the band-7 models’ Constraint and Perceptible).

band7.why: Rarity matches the band-7 M1 models: options 5,327 to 11,243 corrected (Simulated 7,616 corrected, 18,144 raw; mean log 3.91 against 3.88 and 3.84 for 6557f7fc and 7f935017), one band, and the target is a non-first sense (affect = put on) keyed by a mid-frequency word, as Constraint and Perceptible are. But both band-7 M1 models rely on distractor senses that read sensibly in the sentence (Modesty, Composure; Realized), and here Swayed, Perturbed and Afflicted make no sense with “a reserved stateliness of manner” as object, so a student who substitutes rules them out. That move is excluded by design (no loose fits), so it cannot be hardened further; consistent with the b4 M1 verdict.

items.passage: Horses’ blanket preferences appear far from ______. After Cecilie Mejdell and colleagues trained horses to communicate by touching boards displaying symbols for “blanket on” and “blanket off,” the animals requested blanket removal in sunny weather but asked for blankets when conditions turned wet and cold.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Capricious” means changing on a whim, without a clear reason. The text says the horses’ choices followed the weather: blankets off when it was sunny, blankets on when it was wet and cold. Their preferences were therefore far from capricious.

B.why_wrong: The horses’ choices matched the weather consistently, so their preferences were coherent; saying they were “far from coherent” contradicts the text.

C.why_wrong: “Hereditary” means passed down from parents to offspring. The text says nothing about whether horses inherit their blanket preferences; it reports that their requests followed the weather.

D.why_wrong: “Pronounced” means clear and definite. The horses made clear choices, asking for blankets in one kind of weather and not another, so “far from pronounced” contradicts the text.

sources.what: ScienceAlert on Mejdell, Buvik, Jørgensen and Bøe (Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 2016), lead researcher Cecilie Mejdell of the Norwegian Veterinary Institute: horses taught to point to symbols for blanket on, blanket off and no change asked to have a blanket on when the weather was wet and cold and wanted it removed when it was sunny

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal behavior). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (negated frame; the weather-matched choices show the preferences are not whimsical). Distractors: two negation flips (coherent, pronounced) and one unsupported (hereditary; review replaced extravagant, since “far from extravagant” read loosely as modest, reasonable demands fits the weather-matched requests); “fixed” and similar words were avoided because the preferences do change with the weather. Simplified: the third, “no change” symbol and the counts of horses are left out. Raw freq.txt ranks: capricious 11,198; coherent 20,060; hereditary 9,784; pronounced 3,747.

fixes: option C extravagant replaced by hereditary (rank 9,784): “far from extravagant” could be read loosely as modest, reasonable requests, which the weather-matched choices support; why_wrong C rewritten

items.passage: Sagebrush plants appear ______ the chemical signals of their relatives. Richard Karban and colleagues demonstrated that clipped sagebrush releases airborne compounds that help neighboring plants resist herbivores, and that plants respond more vigorously to these volatile cues when the cues originate from close kin.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Partial to” means having a particular liking for or favoring something. The text says sagebrush plants respond more strongly to airborne cues from close relatives than to cues from other plants, so they seem to favor their relatives’ signals.

A.why_wrong: Plants that respond more strongly to their relatives’ cues are not “indifferent to” those signals; the text says the relatives’ signals matter more to them.

B.why_wrong: Plants that respond more strongly to their relatives’ cues, which help them resist herbivores, are drawn to those signals rather than repelled by them.

C.why_wrong: “Imitative of” means copying. The text says plants respond to their relatives’ chemical signals, not that they imitate them.

sources.what: Karban, Shiojiri, Ishizaki, Wetzel and Evans, Kin recognition affects plant communication and defence (Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2013): sagebrush exposed to volatile cues from clipped close relatives suffered less leaf damage over the season than plants exposed to cues from more distant relatives

items.notes: Subject: natural science (plant ecology). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (a stronger response to kin read as favoring them; key a familiar word in its secondary sense, partial to = fond of). Simplified: the experiments’ genetic markers and the camphor and thujone chemotypes are left out. Raw freq.txt ranks: indifferent to 2,479; repelled by 10,635; imitative of 26,701; partial to 8,919.

fixes: passage “herbivorous insects” changed to “herbivores” (the paper reports reduced leaf herbivory, not insects specifically); why_wrong B to match

items.passage: The abstract sculptures in Lebanese artist Saloua Raouda Choucair’s Poems series are ______: each is assembled from separate components that can be stacked in multiple configurations, much as individual stanzas of Arabic poetry can stand independently or be read as part of a larger composition.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Modular” means built from separate units that can be combined in different ways. The text says each sculpture in the Poems series is assembled from separate components that can be stacked in more than one arrangement, like the stanzas of a poem.

A.why_wrong: “Figurative” describes art that represents recognizable figures such as people or animals. The text calls the sculptures abstract, and its clue concerns how they are put together, not what they depict.

C.why_wrong: “Monolithic” means formed from a single large block. The text says each sculpture is made of separate pieces, the opposite of a single block.

D.why_wrong: “Satirical” means mocking or ridiculing. Nothing in the text suggests the sculptures make fun of anything; it describes their structure.

sources.what: e-flux announcement of Tate Modern’s 2013 Saloua Raouda Choucair exhibition: Lebanese artist and a pioneer of abstract art in the Middle East; modular Poems series made from individual pieces that stack together in a flexible way, much like the stanzas of Arabic poetry

Tate, The life and work of Saloua Raouda Choucair: pioneered abstract art in the Middle East; the series she titled “poems”, modular sculptures with parts that stack together in a flexible way; each module, like the stanzas of Arabic poetry, may stand alone or be stacked with others to be read as a whole

items.notes: Subject: humanities (sculpture). Key letter B. Steps: 1 (restatement after the colon), with a medium-band key. Distractors: two reversals (monolithic, and figurative against “abstract”) and one unsupported art word (satirical). Words that would also fit the restatement (composite, segmented, interchangeable) were kept out of the options. Raw freq.txt ranks: figurative 27,434; modular 67,594 (a modern word the old corpus undercounts); monolithic 53,536; satirical 12,736.

fixes: added Tate source: e-flux lacks the passage’s point that stanzas (and modules) can stand alone or be read as a whole

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: During World War I, General John J. Pershing requested permission to hire 100 telephone operators who were ______ to staff a battlefield communications network for American forces in France: the network would have to handle conversations in both French and English, and comparatively few US soldiers spoke French. The women recruited became known as the “Hello Girls.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Bilingual” means able to speak two languages. The text explains why Pershing needed such operators: the network had to handle calls in both French and English, and few US soldiers spoke French.

A.why_wrong: Operators might well need to be “punctual,” or on time, but the reason the text gives concerns languages, not timekeeping.

B.why_wrong: “Reticent” means reluctant to speak. Operators whose job was to handle calls in two languages would need to speak readily, so the text gives no reason to seek reticent ones.

D.why_wrong: “Unflappable” means calm under pressure. That might suit a battlefield job, but the text’s stated reason, calls in both French and English, points to language ability, not temperament.

sources.what: Engineering and Technology History Wiki (IEEE), Hello Girls: Pershing requested permission to hire 100 French-speaking telephone operators; the Signal Corps had to establish a bilingual battlefield telephone system; US soldiers lacked the skills and few spoke French; the workers were commonly called the hello girls

items.notes: Subject: history (World War I). Key letter C. Steps: 1 (cause clue after the colon). Distractors: two plausible qualities for an operator that the stated reason does not support (punctual, unflappable) and one reversal (reticent). Simplified: the request was made in November 1917; recruiting and the later dispute over the operators’ veteran status are left out. Raw freq.txt ranks: punctual 14,728; reticent 11,771; bilingual unseen; unflappable unseen.

items.passage:
The following text is from Edna Lyall’s 1884 novel We Two. Erica’s father, who has been unwell, suggests a nighttime drive to a country retreat.

She was so glad to see him take an interest in anything, and so greatly relieved by his recovery of strength and spirits, that she gladly <u>fell in with</u> the plan, and before long they set off in one of the wagonettes belonging to the Shrub Inn.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “fell in with” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Erica is glad to see her father take an interest in anything and relieved that he is recovering, and right afterward the two set off on the drive he proposed. She “gladly fell in with” his plan, meaning she went along with it.

A.why_wrong: To fall in with someone can mean to meet them by chance, but Erica does not come upon the plan by accident; her father has just proposed it, and she accepts it.

B.why_wrong: Read literally, to fall in is to tumble into something, but nothing in the text involves falling; it describes Erica’s response to a suggestion.

C.why_wrong: Erica is glad and relieved, and the two set off together, so she does not argue against the plan.

sources.what: Text of We Two: A Novel (Edna Lyall, 1884)

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter D. Excerpt is one complete paragraph copied exactly. The intro summarizes the paragraphs before it: Raeburn tells Erica he is “better” and, “looking more like himself than he had done for some days,” proposes driving that night to the “rural retreat”; the paragraph itself mentions his “recovery of strength and spirits”. Distractors: two other senses of the phrase (meet by chance; literally tumble in) and one reversal. The sense “become involved with” was left out because it fits loosely.

items.passage: The Lowell Offering, a literary magazine published in Lowell, Massachusetts, from 1840 to 1845, ______ the writing of young women employed in the city’s cotton mills. According to its title page, the magazine was written entirely by mill workers, and it featured their poetry, fiction, and autobiographical accounts.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Showcased” means displayed or presented to the public. The text says the magazine was written entirely by women who worked in the mills and was filled with their poems, stories, and life accounts, so it presented their writing to readers.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests the women wrote in another language; the magazine printed their own writing.

C.why_wrong: A magazine filled with the mill workers’ own poems and stories published their writing; it did not suppress it.

D.why_wrong: The text says the magazine printed the women’s poems, stories, and accounts, not short summaries of them.

sources.what: Encyclopedia.com, Lowell Offering: a literary magazine written and edited by factory workers in the cotton mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, from 1840 to 1845; title page described it as written exclusively by females employed in the mills; poetic, fictional and autobiographical accounts

items.notes: Subject: humanities (literature and history, a workers’ magazine). Key letter B. Steps: 1 (restatement in the next sentence). Raw freq.txt ranks: translated 6,243; showcased 68,485 (modern word, undercounted); suppressed 4,082; summarized 50,542.

items.passage: Labor organizer Emma Tenayuca withdrew from her public role early in the 1938 pecan shellers’ strike in San Antonio, Texas, but she remained ______. Working behind the scenes, she reviewed reports, consulted with picket captains, and produced leaflets for thousands of workers protesting a reduction in their wages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Active” means busy and involved. Although Tenayuca stepped back from her public role, the text lists what she kept doing behind the scenes: reviewing reports, meeting with picket captains, and writing leaflets.

B.why_wrong: Tenayuca kept helping the strikers by writing leaflets and meeting with picket captains, so she did not remain neutral.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns Tenayuca’s wealth; it describes her work for the strike.

D.why_wrong: The text does not say Tenayuca was afraid; it describes the work she continued to do.

sources.what: UT Arlington Libraries, Emma Tenayuca and the 1938 San Antonio Pecan Shellers’ Strike: a January 1938 pay cut led thousands of shellers to walk out; Tenayuca stepped back on the second day of the strike, was elected honorary strike leader, and continued behind the scenes reviewing reports, meeting picket captains and creating leaflets

items.notes: Subject: history (US labor history). Key letter A. Steps: 1 (restatement after the colon). “Anonymous” and “hidden” were kept out of the options because “behind the scenes” would support them. Simplified: why she stepped back (pressure over her Communist Party ties) and the honorary title are left out. Raw freq.txt ranks: active 2,876; neutral 12,276; wealthy 5,259; fearful 2,955.

items.passage: The glow of a milky sea, a rare phenomenon in which bioluminescent bacteria illuminate the ocean’s surface at night, can be remarkably ______. Satellite images analyzed by Steven Miller and colleagues revealed that one milky sea, encountered by a ship off Somalia in 1995, covered approximately 15,400 square kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Expansive” means covering a wide area. The text says satellite images showed that one milky sea covered roughly 15,400 square kilometers, so these glows can be very large.

A.why_wrong: The text does not say how long a milky sea lasts; it gives the size of the area one covered.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests the glowing water is poisonous; it describes how large an area the glow covered.

C.why_wrong: The text does not describe how quickly a milky sea appears; its detail concerns the size of the glow.

sources.what: Miller et al., Scientific Reports (2021), reviewing the first satellite detection (Miller et al. 2005): the S.S. Lima traversed a milky sea in January 1995, later confirmed from space; the imagery revealed a ~15,400 km2 luminous region; milky seas arise from luminous bacteria with microalgae

Miller, Haddock, Elvidge and Lee, Detection of a bioluminescent milky sea from space (PNAS, 2005): first satellite observations of a milky sea, an area of about 15,400 km2 in the northwestern Indian Ocean, corroborated by the British merchant vessel SS Lima, about 150 nautical miles east of the Somalian coast, January 1995

items.notes: Subject: natural science (oceanography). Key letter D. Steps: 1 (the area figure restates the key). Location “off the coast of Somalia” follows NASA’s account of the same 1995 report (science.nasa.gov, Hunting Milky Seas by Satellite). Raw freq.txt ranks: fleeting 2,773; toxic 49,066; sudden 525; expansive 21,169.

fixes: added the 2005 PNAS paper as source: it is the study the passage describes and the one that places the Lima sighting off Somalia (the 2021 source gives no location)

items.passage: Although it was not discovered until 1988, the ocean bacterium Prochlorococcus is extraordinarily ______. Earth’s oceans are estimated to hold about three billion billion billion of the tiny cells, which makes Prochlorococcus by far the most abundant photosynthetic organism on the planet, according to Sallie Chisholm, the MIT biologist who identified it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Plentiful” means existing in great numbers. The text says the oceans hold about three billion billion billion Prochlorococcus cells, more than any other photosynthetic organism.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says Prochlorococcus is poisonous; it describes how many of the cells there are.

B.why_wrong: “Scarce” means rare. The text calls Prochlorococcus the most abundant photosynthetic organism on the planet, the opposite of rare.

D.why_wrong: The text calls the cells tiny and notes that they were not discovered until 1988, so they are not easy to see.

items.passage: Strangers asked for a small favor do not ______ as often as people expect. In studies by Francis Flynn and Vanessa Lake, participants who asked strangers to fill out a questionnaire or do similar favors consistently overestimated how many people they would need to approach before enough of them said yes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Decline” here means to say no to a request. The participants consistently overestimated how many people they would have to ask before enough said yes, which means strangers turned them down less often than they expected.

B.why_wrong: The participants needed fewer strangers than they expected, so strangers agreed more often than expected, not less; saying strangers do not agree as often as people expect reverses the finding.

C.why_wrong: The text is about whether strangers said yes to a request, not about whether they listened.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns strangers complaining; it compares how often they said yes with how often participants expected them to.
